---
name: xsk-execute-plan
description: Execute a small plan or request as context-isolated subagent tasks sharing one writable workspace, tracked in a .xsk/runs/ ledger, with one confirmation gate, no per-task code review, and unified acceptance. Explicit invocation only.
---

# xsk-execute-plan

Execute a small, decision-light plan or request through context-isolated subagent tasks that share the same writable workspace, so the main conversation keeps only compact results instead of file contents. A persistent run ledger under `.xsk/runs/` records every task and its acceptance state, so a mid-run context compression loses nothing that matters.

It fits tasks that are simple to decide but heavy to execute: the work reads and writes far more content than the task description itself (several files, several steps). Its evidence bookkeeping carries a real fixed cost, since a Git baseline, path-state fingerprints, and anchored checkpoints are all established before the first task runs, so the work has to be large enough to earn that overhead. Anything small enough to inspect directly, including a one-file tweak or a single command, is cheaper done inline.

## When to use

This skill is explicitly invoked only: `/xsk-execute-plan`, a direct request such as "use xsk-execute-plan to run this", or the user's selection of the `xsk-execute-plan` next action offered by `xsk-think`. As a deliberate local rule that overrides the shared intent-matching convention below, it never self-triggers on execution intent, so it cannot collide with a harness's own plan or execution modes.

Selection from `xsk-think` is an explicit invocation of this skill, but invocation starts intake only. It never means immediate task dispatch and never bypasses this skill's task-breakdown and acceptance confirmation gate.

It accepts two kinds of input:

- a concrete execution plan, such as an approved `xsk-think` design
- a small plain-language request that needs no real design work first

## How it works

**1. Intake, ground lightly, and confirm dispatch capability.** Restate the goal in one sentence. A concrete plan (such as an approved `xsk-think` design) is taken as given; a small plain-language request gets a quick scan of the directly relevant code and config, not a full design pass. Derive the run slug from the goal line using the pattern `^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`.

Before offering any recovery choice and before opening a run ledger, verify that the current harness can dispatch at least one subagent that can write to the same workspace and return a compact result. Also require a durable evidence-anchor store for the main workflow, kept outside the Git worktree, addressable by repository identity and run slug without trusting the workspace ledger, and able to survive context compaction and session recovery. Do not require or claim that it is write-protected from subagents or project commands. On every platform this skill targets they run as the same user with the same filesystem access, so no such boundary exists to ask for, and asserting one would fabricate the very guarantee the evidence chain is supposed to earn. What the store actually buys is real but bounded: living outside the worktree keeps it clear of the paths tasks and commands are told to write, and the hash chain below detects accidental divergence, interrupted writes, and inconsistent state. Neither detects deliberate tampering by anything that has write access, and neither may be reported as if it did. If writable-workspace subagent dispatch or that store is unavailable, stop before offering a recovery choice or writing a ledger. Recommend direct execution, or return to `xsk-think` to reduce, split, or revise the plan. Never silently degrade `xsk-execute-plan` into inline execution. These are one-time capability checks, not preconditions re-tested before each ledger line.

**2. Establish a committed Git baseline, resolve prior state, then preflight the hard rules.** Run `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` and `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` before offering a recovery choice or writing a ledger. If the workspace is not a Git worktree or has no valid `HEAD` commit, stop without writing anything and explain that `xsk-execute-plan` requires a committed Git baseline. A non-Git directory and an unborn repository are unsupported; never invent an empty base commit or claim that an unavailable actual diff was verified. For a new run or confirmed restart, record the full current `HEAD` object ID as both the immutable original base commit and the initial last reconciled `HEAD`. For resume or reuse, read both values from the existing ledger and protected anchor, verify that both objects still exist, and never replace the immutable original base with current `HEAD`. If current `HEAD` differs from the last reconciled `HEAD`, reuse is disabled until the movement is reconciled. A resume may continue only when the last reconciled `HEAD` is still an ancestor of current `HEAD` and the complete forward interval passes the reconciliation below; otherwise report repository movement as interruption ambiguity before any further dispatch and require explicit resolution or a restart against current `HEAD`.

The immutable original base commit is the acceptance anchor; the last reconciled `HEAD` is only a repository-movement cursor. Re-run `git rev-parse --verify HEAD` immediately before every task dispatch, after every subagent returns before attributing its writes, before unified acceptance, and immediately before writing the final fingerprint. When it equals the last reconciled `HEAD`, carry on. When `git merge-base --is-ancestor <last reconciled HEAD> HEAD` succeeds, do not advance the cursor yet. Before accepting the movement or updating the last reconciled `HEAD`, enumerate and record the ordered commit IDs in `<last reconciled HEAD>..HEAD` and each commit's complete parent-relative changed-path record, including path status, before and after object IDs, and paths changed and later reverted inside the interval. Reconcile every committed path through the same allowed-path, scope-drift, dirty-overlap preservation, and user-ownership rules as task output. When this check follows a task return, compare the interval receipt with that attempt's start and returned evidence before attributing a committed path to the task. A clean worktree after a commit is not evidence that the interval was in scope. An undeclared committed path that is not proven to be concurrent user work enters the scope-drift flow. Only after the complete interval is reconciled and the user confirms the movement may an anchored ledger update advance the last reconciled `HEAD`; it never changes the immutable original base. Advancing the movement cursor never advances the acceptance baseline: unified acceptance, the implementation diff, and the final workspace fingerprint remain anchored to the immutable original base and also bind the final reconciled `HEAD`. When the last reconciled `HEAD` is no longer an ancestor, history was rewritten under the run: do not dispatch, attribute output, verify, or mint a fingerprint, preserve the worktree, keep any returned task nonterminal with repository-movement ambiguity and observable path states, and require explicit resolution or restart.

If `.xsk/runs/<slug>.md` already exists:

First resolve the candidate input identity. If any replacement `source`, goal, or complete plan or request text is supplied, compute the candidate only from those new values and never substitute the persisted preimage for a missing or inconvenient field. If the user explicitly selects this existing run and asks only to resume or reuse it without supplying replacement input, look up its protected anchor independently of the ledger, verify the persisted input preimage's anchored artifact hash, recorded decimal byte length, and input identity, and use those exact saved bytes as the candidate. This is the context-compaction recovery path, not permission to infer a different request. A missing, unreadable, length-mismatched, digest-mismatched, or unanchored input preimage makes resume and reuse unavailable; require restart and a newly confirmed envelope.

- With `status: running` or `status: failed`, compare the resolved candidate input identity with the recorded one before offering resume. Only an exact match may offer the user resume or restart. If it differs or uses an unrecognized scheme, resume is unavailable: present the old task state as history, offer only restart, and require the replacement execution envelope to be rebuilt and explicitly confirmed through steps 3 and 4 before any old task can be dispatched. On a matching resume, continue from the current worktree, never by rolling source files back: keep `done` tasks, re-dispatch only unfinished tasks whose state is pending or failed, and resume reconciliation for every task whose state is `reconciling` before any new dispatch. A task left at `reconciling` has returned and must not be re-dispatched: verify its anchored post-return checkpoint, continue its incomplete touched-path, preservation, and scope decisions, and never enter unified acceptance while any task remains `reconciling`. A task left at `in-flight` was dispatched and never reported back, so its writes may be fully, partly, or not at all applied: never re-dispatch it blind. Inspect its allowed paths, report what is already there, and ask the user whether to re-dispatch it as the next attempt, move the existing state to `reconciling`, or fail it after reconciliation. Choosing the existing state never marks it `done` directly. If all tasks are terminal, resume at unified acceptance and reporting instead of dispatching them again.
- Restart uses the current worktree without reset or rollback, but it does not erase provenance that the old run can still prove. Before replacing the old ledger or companion artifacts, compare every old actual-touched path's current state with its most recent anchored terminal `done` or `failed` fingerprint. An exact match retains prior-run-output attribution for the old run's contribution only and never transfers ownership of pre-run dirty or ignored content. Show all exact matches and ask the user to select exactly which matching prior-run output paths the restarted run may supersede. Record each selected path, old task and attempt, terminal fingerprint, and carried dirty-overlap preservation reference in the replacement envelope. Matching paths not selected remain protected existing state. A missing or mismatching terminal fingerprint makes the checkpoint-to-restart difference user state or ambiguity: preserve that difference as a new dirty-overlap baseline when it can be derived, otherwise protect the entire current path state, and never include it in the supersede selection. Persist the carryover record and required baseline evidence under a new anchored run generation before replacing the old workspace artifacts; retain the old protected anchor until that transaction commits. The restart records current `HEAD` as its new immutable original base and initial last reconciled `HEAD`, then rebuilds and re-confirms every other envelope field.
- With `status: done`, compare exactly two identities, both recomputed from anchored material that still exists: the resolved candidate input identity against the recorded one, and a freshly computed workspace fingerprint against the one recorded in `## Result`, matching the exact path set as well as every path-state fingerprint. Do not ask the run to re-derive the old execution envelope and match it: a fresh decomposition of the same plan will not reproduce the recorded task definitions verbatim, so that comparison could never pass and would only dress a blanket refusal as a check.

  When the input identity differs, is missing, or cannot be reproduced through the supplied replacement input or verified persisted preimage, present the old result as history only and offer only a new run with a newly confirmed envelope: the old task outputs do not prove that a revised plan was implemented. When the input identity matches but the workspace fingerprint differs or is missing, reuse stays off the table, but fresh unified acceptance against the current state may be offered alongside a new run, provided all anchored historical baseline and terminal checkpoint evidence is intact; apply the resume ambiguity rules before verification. A run with incomplete ignored-path coverage has no acceptance fingerprint and is never eligible for reuse. Fresh acceptance may report current checks, but it cannot reconstruct the missing pre-run ignored state, produce a verified fingerprint, or promote that run to verified; offer a new run or restart with intact ignored coverage when reusable proof is required. Only when both identities and the protected evidence anchor match may reuse without dispatch be offered alongside a new run. A result that fails any required comparison must never be reported as verified. A `done` run whose result was already reported and consumed may instead be retired by deleting its workspace artifacts and protected anchor in one explicit retirement operation: stale partial evidence is not reusable.

A resume reuses the execution envelope recorded in the ledger, including its pre-existing dirty-path baseline, only after the anchor verifies every artifact: the worktree now also holds this run's own writes, so recapturing that baseline would misread them as the user's work. Before dispatching anything, compare current versioned path-state fingerprints with the recorded dirty baselines and terminal task-output fingerprints. A dirty path whose fingerprint still matches is untouched user work. Matching the most recent terminal `done` or `failed` fingerprint proves only that the task-end state is unchanged; path membership or a compact result alone is never proof of run ownership, and a match never transfers ownership of pre-run dirty content. A dirty-overlap path remains subject to its separately recorded user-change preservation proof. Anything with no matching baseline, or whose latest task-output fingerprint no longer matches, is a user change or ambiguity that appeared during the interruption. Report it and treat it as the user's, never as this run's to overwrite. A resume does not re-run the confirmation gate. If ordinary envelope fields do not cover every unfinished task but all anchored historical baseline and checkpoint evidence is intact, extend the envelope and re-confirm it through steps 3 and 4 before dispatching anything. A missing or invalid original base, reconciled-HEAD receipt, dirty-overlap baseline, companion artifact, input identity or preimage, evidence anchor, or required terminal output checkpoint cannot be reconstructed from the current worktree during resume. The same is true of a missing ignored-state baseline, coverage record, or acceptance-command checkpoint needed to attribute post-command writes. Report the affected paths as ambiguous and require explicit resolution or restart; never recapture current state and call it the original baseline. A restart follows the carryover procedure above and rebuilds and re-confirms the envelope.

The resume, restart, or reuse choice is exceptional recovery, not the normal confirmation gate. A prior `failed` run is never overwritten silently.

Scan `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, and any repo rules or config for constraints that would forbid or force a choice. Keep this brief: it is a check, not a study.

**3. Decompose and define the execution envelope.** Produce an ordered task list with at least one entry and record each task's dependencies and execution order. Define the acceptance criteria before anything executes. For every task, name its expected write paths, the tolerated side-effect paths that correct work legitimately touches (regenerated output, lockfiles, formatter fallout), and the project verification commands that cover it. For every verification command, also name its own expected and tolerated write footprint, including snapshots, generated files, and formatter output, or write `none` when it is expected to be read-only.

Record the input identity as `xsk-execute-plan-input-v1:sha256:<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>`. Build the preimage by writing the literal `source` value, the exact goal line, and the complete plan or request text exactly as supplied, in that order, each followed by one newline, into a temporary file. Hash the exact bytes with an executed SHA-256 implementation (`shasum -a 256`, `sha256sum`, or Node's built-in `crypto`); never write a digest from inspection. Always persist the exact preimage bytes used for the identity, including the `sha256` form, at `.xsk/runs/<slug>.baseline/input-v1`. Record its relative path, decimal byte length, and matching SHA-256 identity in the ledger, and bind the file into the protected artifact anchor. If SHA-256 cannot actually be computed, stop before the normal gate rather than inventing an identity or an unverifiable fallback. A missing or unrecognized scheme is an identity failure, never permission to guess another serialization.

Capture the pre-existing dirty paths before dispatch. Also establish an ignored-state baseline and record which of three scopes it has.

`Ignored-path coverage: footprint` is the default. It covers every ignored path inside a declared task or verification-command footprint, plus any additional ignored root the user names at the gate. `Ignored-path coverage: repository-wide` additionally enumerates and fingerprints the whole worktree's ignored namespace, excluding Git metadata and only this run's independently anchored artifacts, and repeats that enumeration in every post-writer scan. Offer repository-wide when the user wants assurance beyond the declared footprints, and say what it costs: one dependency or build directory routinely holds far more files than the entire run touches, and the walk repeats after every writer. Record `Ignored-path coverage: incomplete` with the covered roots, the uncovered remainder, and the reason whenever a selected root cannot be enumerated or fingerprinted. Never treat unobserved ignored state as unchanged.

Within every covered root, use the repository's Git ignore rules plus a filesystem walk that does not follow symlinks, consolidate nested entries into a minimal set of roots, and record deterministic recursive entry manifests that are sufficient to identify changed descendants.

Footprint coverage supports a verified acceptance, but its scope claim is bounded and must be reported that way: it proves that nothing strayed within the covered roots, never that nothing was written elsewhere in the ignored namespace. Only repository-wide coverage carries the unbounded claim, and neither may be described as the other. Incomplete coverage is the failing scope: it permits execution and ordinary checks, but it disables verified acceptance, acceptance-fingerprint production, and reuse.

Treat every pre-existing ignored path, including one outside all task footprints, as user state because Git cannot supply its baseline. Every comparable path-state fingerprint uses the versioned form `xsk-execute-plan-path-state-v1:sha256:<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>`. Its preimage is the exact JSON object shown below, serialized with the RFC 8785 JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS), encoded as UTF-8 without a BOM, and hashed by an executed SHA-256 implementation. Every displayed key is mandatory, including the empty index tombstone, and no undisplayed key is allowed:

```json
{"git_object_format":"sha1","index":[],"path":"relative/path","schema":"xsk-execute-plan-path-state-v1","worktree":{"kind":"absent"}}
```

`git_object_format` is exactly `sha1` or `sha256` as returned by `git rev-parse --show-object-format`; any other result is unsupported by this schema. `path` is the repository-relative slash-separated path with no Unicode normalization. `index` is either the empty-array absent-index tombstone or entries of the exact shape `{"mode":"100644","oid":"<lowercase hexadecimal object ID>","stage":0}`, sorted by numeric `stage`; obtain `mode` and `oid` from Git's stage entry without substituting worktree data. Git status, rename, and copy records may discover candidate paths only: no derived status field enters this preimage, and fingerprint both sides of a discovered rename or copy as separate paths. The `worktree` value is exactly one of the following tagged objects, with no additional keys:

```json
{"kind":"absent"}
{"byte_length":0,"kind":"regular","mode":"100644","sha256":"<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>"}
{"kind":"symlink","mode":"120777","target_base64":"<RFC 4648 base64 with padding>"}
{"kind":"directory","manifest":"xsk-execute-plan-directory-manifest-v1:sha256:<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>","mode":"040755"}
```

Encode stages and byte lengths as JSON integers. An index mode is Git's exact six-character ASCII octal mode. A filesystem mode is the six-character, zero-padded ASCII octal encoding of `lstat(2).st_mode & 0177777`, with no umask, executable-bit, or file-type normalization; use the same rule for directory-manifest entries. Hash regular worktree files from their raw bytes. Encode the exact raw symlink-target bytes as base64 without following the link. A Git blob object ID is index evidence and is never a substitute for the regular worktree file's SHA-256.

A directory uses the exact JSON object `{"entries":[],"schema":"xsk-execute-plan-directory-manifest-v1"}`, with `entries` populated by the exact variants below. Apply the same JCS, UTF-8, and executed SHA-256 rules, and record its identity as `xsk-execute-plan-directory-manifest-v1:sha256:<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>`. Every displayed entry key is mandatory for that variant, and no additional key is allowed:

```json
{"kind":"directory","mode":"040755","path":"empty-directory"}
{"byte_length":0,"kind":"regular","mode":"100644","path":"file","sha256":"<64 lowercase hexadecimal characters>"}
{"kind":"symlink","mode":"120777","path":"link","target_base64":"<RFC 4648 base64 with padding>"}
```

The entries array contains every descendant, including empty directories but excluding the manifest root itself. Each `path` is non-empty, slash-separated, relative to that root, and not Unicode-normalized. Do not follow symlinks. Sort entries by the UTF-8 byte order of their `path` values before serialization. Store the canonical directory manifest, not only its digest, when later changed-descendant attribution depends on it. Sort acceptance path sets by the same UTF-8 byte order. If a required path is unreadable, has an unsupported node type, has an unsupported Git object format, lacks the required mode source, or cannot be represented exactly by this format, its fingerprint is unavailable: record ambiguity and do not resume, reuse, or mint a verified acceptance fingerprint from it. A status label such as `MM` is never a substitute for the exact index entries, because index content can change while that label and the worktree bytes stay the same. These paths belong to the user, not to this run. A bare path list cannot show later whether those changes survived, so record one fingerprint per path or consolidated ignored root.

If an expected or tolerated write path overlaps dirty or pre-existing ignored user state, a whole-file hash alone is not sufficient: after legitimate task edits, a different hash cannot prove whether the user's original change survived. Overlap includes exact equality and ancestor or descendant containment after path normalization, without following symlinks. For every overlap, prepare a comparable preservation baseline before dispatch. Preserve the index and worktree layers separately with binary-capable base-to-index and index-to-worktree patches, or with the full staged blobs, exact index entries, and full worktree content and path state. Plan to store it and any large ignored-state manifests inline in the ledger, or in an immutable `.xsk/runs/<slug>.baseline/` companion referenced by relative path and hash from the ledger when inline Markdown is unsuitable. Do not write either run artifact before the normal gate; immediately after approval, persist and hash-check all baseline evidence before any task becomes `in-flight`. Call out the ignored-path coverage and each overlap with its preservation-baseline reference explicitly in the confirmation envelope.

Mark every task that has a UI surface and record for it the reference (a design link or image), the target platform (Android, web, or desktop), and how to render and screenshot it. Also list any external, destructive, irreversible, remote, dependency-introducing, or platform-permission action that the plan may require. Write `none` when a category has no such action.

**4. One normal confirmation gate.** Show the user the complete execution envelope: the immutable original base and initial reconciled `HEAD`, ordered tasks and dependency order, acceptance criteria, expected write paths, tolerated side-effect paths, verification commands, pre-existing dirty paths, ignored-path coverage, versioned path-state fingerprints and overlap preservation-baseline references, input-preimage storage, prior-run carryover if any, UI advisory, and flagged exceptional actions. Get one explicit go-ahead. This is the only checkpoint on the normal path; a recovery choice in step 2 is exceptional. Even an approved `xsk-think` plan passes through this gate. Selecting `xsk-execute-plan` from `xsk-think` explicitly invokes this skill, but it does not approve this envelope or authorize immediate dispatch.

The workflow gate authorizes only the confirmed, local, reversible workspace changes. It never authorizes a new product decision, scope expansion, dependency introduction, external or remote mutation, destructive or irreversible action, or a platform permission prompt. If any of those is planned or appears during execution, stop before it and obtain focused user authorization. Before dispatch, record each granted exception in the execution envelope with its exact action, target, assigned task, scope, limits, and permitted attempts. The exception authorizes only those recorded terms; it does not carry to another task, retry, verifier, or fix task unless the recorded terms explicitly include it. A newly discovered decision that changes implementation also returns to the user. These exceptional authorizations do not weaken the single normal workflow gate.

**5. Open the ledger, then dispatch context-isolated tasks.** Only after the normal gate passes, write the run ledger `.xsk/runs/<slug>.md` with `status: running`:

```markdown
---
status: running | done | failed
slug: <slug>
created_at: <ISO date>
source: plan | request
---

# <goal in one line>

## Execution Envelope
- Original base commit: <immutable full Git object ID captured at run or restart start>
- Reconciled HEAD: <initial object ID; each reconciled interval with ordered commits, complete per-commit path receipts, attribution, resolution, and reason>
- Input identity: <xsk-execute-plan-input-v1:sha256:64-lowercase-hex from an executed SHA-256 implementation>
- Input preimage: <.xsk/runs/<slug>.baseline/input-v1; decimal byte length; matching SHA-256 identity>
- Path-state scheme: <xsk-execute-plan-path-state-v1 and xsk-execute-plan-directory-manifest-v1>
- Evidence anchor: <xsk-execute-plan-anchor-v1 external handle; run generation; committed sequence>
- Dependency order: <task order>
- Expected write paths: <paths by task and verification command>
- Tolerated side-effect paths: <paths by task and verification command, or none>
- Verification commands: <commands>
- Pre-existing dirty paths: <path-state fingerprint per path; overlap preservation-baseline reference and hash, or none>
- Ignored-path coverage: <footprint or repository-wide with baseline roots and hashes, or incomplete with covered roots, uncovered remainder, and reason>
- Prior-run carryover: <old anchored run identity; selected supersedable paths with task, attempt, terminal fingerprint, and preservation reference; protected checkpoint-to-restart state, or none>
- UI advisory: <task details or none>
- Exceptional actions and authorizations: <action, target, assigned task, scope, limits, permitted attempts, and pending or granted status, or none>

## Acceptance
- [ ] <criterion>

## Tasks
1. [pending|in-flight|reconciling|done|failed] (attempt <n>) <full task description, self-contained enough to re-dispatch, with dependencies, allowed write paths, and acceptance items> - <attempt-start fingerprints; anchored post-return checkpoint; unresolved reconciliation or decision; compact result; actual touched paths; terminal output path-state fingerprints; dirty-overlap preservation result>

## Result
(after all tasks: per-criterion pass/fail/skipped, verifier result, failures, actual touched paths, leftovers)
Acceptance fingerprint: <immutable original base commit; final reconciled HEAD; ignored-path coverage state; exact UTF-8-byte-sorted path set from Git-different, expected, tolerated, and actual-touched paths; each path's xsk-execute-plan-path-state-v1 fingerprint at acceptance time>
```

Anchor every ledger, input preimage, baseline, directory manifest, and other run companion with an external record using schema `xsk-execute-plan-anchor-v1`. The anchor binds the canonical repository identity, slug, run generation, monotonic sequence, immutable original base, last reconciled `HEAD`, input identity, SHA-256 of the ledger's exact bytes, and an exact sorted artifact manifest containing each companion's relative path, node type, canonical mode, decimal byte length, and raw-byte SHA-256. It also binds the previous committed anchor digest so revisions form a hash chain. Find this record in the anchor store by repository identity, slug, and generation; a handle copied from the workspace ledger is never the authority, because the ledger is one of the artifacts under inspection.

Every intentional run-artifact mutation uses a recoverable two-phase anchored checkpoint. Construct the complete next artifact bytes first; append a protected pending anchor revision that carries both the previous committed hashes and the intended next hashes; atomically replace the workspace artifacts; recompute their exact hashes; then promote the pending revision to committed. Dispatch a subagent, run a project command or verifier, or wait for user resolution only after the matching anchor revision is committed. On recovery, a pending revision may be finalized only when the workspace artifacts match its intended hashes, or discarded only when they still match the previous committed hashes; any other state is an evidence-integrity failure.

Verify the committed anchor against every run artifact before and after every subagent dispatch, project command, and fresh verifier; before consuming baseline evidence; and before resume, reuse, unified acceptance, or final fingerprinting. A mismatch means the artifacts and the anchor have diverged, from an interrupted write, an outside edit, or a bug. It is an evidence-integrity failure whatever the cause, and the cause is not something the chain can tell you: preserve the worktree, do not trust or update the workspace ledger as proof, and do not dispatch, attribute output, accept, reuse, or produce an acceptance fingerprint. Record the failure in the anchor store when the ledger itself is untrusted. Ledger and companion paths may be excluded from the implementation diff only after this independent anchor check passes. A reusable `done` run keeps its anchor; explicit retirement removes workspace artifacts and the protected anchor together.

`source: plan` means the input was a concrete plan; `source: request` means a small plain-language request, not a `.xsk/requirements/` document. The complete plan or request is always recoverable from the anchored input preimage. Every `## Tasks` entry carries the full task description as confirmed at the gate; a one-line stub would make resuming meaningless once the session context is gone. Immediately before persisting the approved ledger, input preimage, and baseline artifacts, revalidate every pre-run path-state fingerprint; if one changed while confirmation was pending, update the envelope and obtain a replacement confirmation before dispatch. Persist all initial run artifacts through the anchored checkpoint before any task becomes `in-flight`. Ensure `.xsk/.gitignore` contains the line `runs/` (create `.xsk/` and `.xsk/.gitignore` if absent; append the line only if it is missing; never overwrite an existing `.xsk/.gitignore`). The workspace run artifacts are transient execution state, not deliverables: never offer to commit them. Overwrite or remove existing run state only through the recovery choice in step 2, including the retirement of a reported `done` run offered there.

Subagents are isolated from the main conversation's context, not from one another's filesystem. They share the same writable workspace. Each task goes to one subagent with a self-contained prompt containing the applicable hard rules, the full task and acceptance items, its allowed and expected write paths, required dependency results, and a default prohibition on dependency introduction, remote or external actions, destructive or irreversible actions, and platform permission prompts. When a task has a granted exception recorded in the envelope, copy its exact action, target, scope, limits, and permitted attempts into that task's prompt as the sole exception. Keep the prohibition for everything else, and require the subagent to stop and return without acting if it would exceed the recorded exception. If the exact exception cannot be passed to the assigned task, do not dispatch it. Require the subagent to return a compact result, verification evidence, and its actual touched paths.

Order tasks by dependency. A task's write footprint is its expected write paths together with its tolerated side-effect paths: a shared lockfile or regenerated index counts even when the two tasks own different source files. Run tasks in parallel only when their footprints do not overlap and neither footprint creates ambiguity with a pre-existing dirty path; tasks with authorized external or remote actions also run serially unless their recorded targets and limits prove that they cannot conflict. When in doubt, run them serially, since parallel subagents share the same files. Before every dispatch, compare the complete footprint with its latest trusted pre-run baseline or terminal task checkpoint. Also compare the in-scope ignored roots and their manifests with the latest trusted ignored-state checkpoint. Any mismatch since that checkpoint is new user work or ambiguity: pause, protect it from the next task, and require focused resolution and an updated confirmation when the envelope changes. Never fold it silently into the old preservation proof.

The ledger is write-ahead: in the same anchored write that sets a task's line to `in-flight` with its attempt number, record path-state fingerprints for its complete footprint, the current Git changed-path inventory, and the current ignored-state checkpoint, then dispatch it. These attempt-start records let the main workflow independently derive and validate Git-visible, committed, covered-ignored, and in-footprint changes while reconciling the subagent's report. After the subagent returns and the external anchor still matches, the first post-return checkpoint changes only `in-flight` to `reconciling` and persists the reported outcome and compact result, current Git changed-path inventory, current covered ignored scan, and observable fingerprints for the complete footprint. A self-reported failure also enters `reconciling`; it is not terminal until its partial output is attributed. Then rescan every covered ignored root and compare every root manifest with the attempt-start checkpoint; repository-wide coverage also repeats the whole-namespace enumeration. A changed existing ignored descendant or a newly created ignored path under those roots is an independently detected touched path and enters the scope-drift flow even when the subagent omitted it. If a covered root becomes unreadable, downgrade the scope to incomplete, record the uncovered namespace and resulting ambiguity, mark every acceptance criterion that depended on it `skipped` with that reason, and report it prominently. Incomplete coverage never passes as verified and requires `Acceptance fingerprint: not produced`, so the run cannot be reused; it does not by itself fail a run whose own observable criteria are otherwise met. `reconciling` is nonterminal and blocks dependent dispatch and unified acceptance. Recording only a terminal state after a task finishes would let an interruption between return and reconciliation leave unresolved work looking complete. Between tasks there is no code review and no acceptance run. The main conversation records each task's compact result, path checkpoints, and preservation evidence, all of it produced by tools rather than by reading file contents, and it judges nothing about the implementation until unified acceptance.

While the task is `reconciling`, independently derive every detectable actual touched path from the immutable original base, reconciled commit-range receipts, attempt-start records, current Git state, ignored-state comparison, and the subagent report, including paths that are now absent; reconcile these sources rather than trusting the report alone. Capture a candidate terminal output path-state fingerprint for every one and update the trusted ignored-state checkpoint after reconciling any ignored changes. A failed task can leave partial output, so a failed outcome requires the same evidence as a successful one. If a path or complete touched set cannot be fingerprinted, record the ambiguity in an anchored `reconciling` checkpoint and pause before dispatching dependents; never turn a path name into provenance by assumption. For a path touched by multiple terminal tasks, retain every checkpoint and use the most recent terminal fingerprint as the comparison point on resume.

For every touched dirty-overlap path, compare the immutable-original-base state, saved pre-run index and worktree patches or full snapshots, and post-task index and worktree states after the task returns. Record concrete preservation evidence showing that the pre-existing staged and unstaged user changes survived. A changed whole-file hash or an unchanged two-letter Git status is not that evidence. If the comparison shows loss, or cannot prove preservation, keep the task `reconciling`, set its provisional outcome to `failed` for preservation ambiguity, keep the worktree intact, pause before dispatching dependents, and ask the user how to resolve it; do not mark the task `done` or claim that the user change was preserved. If the task failed for another reason, still record the output fingerprint and preservation result before stopping its dependents. Never silently restore one version over another.

Compare every task's actual touched paths, including reconciled committed paths, with its confirmed allowed paths. Never revert an unexpected path automatically. A path the confirmed envelope already lists as a tolerated side effect is recorded in the ledger and the run carries on. Any other unexpected path is scope drift: pause before dispatching that task's dependents, keep the task `reconciling`, persist the unresolved paths and pending decision in an anchored checkpoint, keep the worktree intact, report the path and what the task wrote there, and ask the user once whether to accept it into scope or fail the task. Accepting records the path in the envelope and resolves that item; failing sets the provisional task outcome to failed and stops its dependents. That question is an exception check against the confirmed envelope, not the per-task code review this skill omits. When a task otherwise fails, stop its dependents, keep what finished, and report honestly. No pretended atomicity, no unbounded auto-fixing.

Only after the actual touched-path set and terminal output fingerprints are complete, every dirty-overlap preservation result is recorded, every committed-path attribution is reconciled, and every scope item and user decision is resolved may one anchored ledger write atomically change `reconciling` to `done` or `failed` and record the compact result and all terminal evidence. Never write a terminal task state earlier. A resume continues this reconciliation from its latest anchored checkpoint and never skips a `reconciling` task to enter acceptance.

Any accepted scope drift or separately authorized action changes the final execution envelope, and its exact authorization terms belong in it. Any functional or UI fix attempt adds a full task definition and dependency to the final ordered task list. Persist those changes before further dispatch and again before final acceptance, so `## Result` describes the effective tasks, acceptance criteria, and envelope that actually produced the result rather than the ones first confirmed.

**6. Accept once, after all tasks.** Two tiers with different weight.

- Functional acceptance is a real signal. First run the project's own verification commands (tests, lint, build) and read the output. Immediately before each command, persist an anchored acceptance-command checkpoint containing the command, current Git changed-path inventory, full path-state fingerprints for its declared write footprint, and the ignored-state checkpoint. After each command returns and the protected artifact anchor still matches, derive and fingerprint every detectable write, including ignored, generated, snapshot, formatter, staged, committed, deleted, and type-changed output. Reconcile any forward `HEAD` interval before attributing command output. In the same next anchored ledger write, record the command's exit result and compact output evidence, actual touched paths, terminal fingerprints, and overlap result. Reconcile those writes through the same allowed-path, scope-drift, dirty-overlap preservation, and ignored-coverage rules as a task before continuing. A command failure does not excuse this reconciliation. Only after the project commands and all of their writes have been reconciled, dispatch a fresh verifier that did not implement any task. Give it the confirmed goal, acceptance criteria, execution envelope, immutable original base commit, final reconciled `HEAD`, complete reconciled commit-range receipts, pre-existing dirty-path fingerprints, covered ignored-state baseline and post-command scan, saved index and worktree overlap patches or full snapshots, recorded overlap-preservation evidence, terminal task-output and acceptance-command fingerprints, actual touched paths, command output evidence, and the post-command actual diff derived against the immutable original base commit and pre-run index and worktree states. The diff and path list must cover staged, unstaged, committed, every detected ignored touch, untracked, deleted, and type-changed paths; construct an explicit before/after representation for paths ordinary Git diff omits. Exclude Git metadata and anchored run artifacts from that implementation diff only after the external anchor matches; include `.xsk/.gitignore` when this run changed it. The verifier checks the implementation against the goal and criteria, independently proves that every dirty-overlap staged and unstaged user change survived, verifies committed-path attribution, scope, and leftovers, and returns evidence without modifying files. Missing or inconclusive overlap evidence is a functional failure, not a pass inferred from hashes or status labels. Footprint coverage verifies scope within its covered roots and must be reported with that bound stated; only repository-wide coverage supports an unbounded ignored-scope claim. Incomplete coverage is not a failure by itself: it marks every criterion that depended on the lost roots `skipped`, forces `Acceptance fingerprint: not produced`, disables reuse, and can never be reported as verified. A verifier mismatch or command failure is also reported as a functional failure. Permit at most one bounded fix attempt for unified functional acceptance, then rerun the project commands, reconcile their writes, and repeat the fresh-verifier check once in that order; never loop. Dispatch that fix as its own write-ahead ledger task under the full step 5 contract: allowed paths, the drift comparison, overlap preservation, terminal output fingerprints, and the same scoped-authority contract, copying only an exact granted exception assigned to that fix task and prohibiting everything else. When the project has no runnable verification commands at all, record the command-backed acceptance criteria as `skipped` and state "functional acceptance not run" prominently in the report: `skipped` is non-failing but must never look like `pass`, the fresh verifier does not turn skipped command checks into passes, and a run with zero runnable gates must never look verified.
- UI fidelity acceptance is warning-level, never a gate. Run it only for tasks marked with a UI surface, and only when the environment can render the UI and capture a screenshot; otherwise record the affected acceptance criteria as `skipped` and use the single line "UI acceptance skipped: cannot render or screenshot here", which is not a failure, blocks nothing, and asks nothing of the user. When it runs: render, screenshot, compare against the design reference, and list concrete deviations (spacing, color, alignment, missing elements, overflow), delegating rendering, screenshots, and visual comparison to existing tools rather than building any. Dispatch a fix subagent scoped to exactly those deviations, re-render, and re-compare, at most 2 rounds by default (the user may set another bound at invocation). Every UI fix round is dispatched as its own write-ahead ledger task under the full step 5 contract too: allowed paths, the drift comparison, and the same scoped-authority contract, copying only an exact granted exception assigned to that UI fix task and prohibiting everything else. Any deviation that survives the last round goes into the report as a warning for the user to weigh; it never fails the run and never gates anything. After the last UI fix round that changed files, rerun the project's relevant functional verification commands (tests, lint, build), reconcile their writes, and only then dispatch a fresh verifier against the updated post-command diff before deriving final status; discard any earlier functional result. A revalidation failure is a functional acceptance failure and sets the ledger to `status: failed`.

After any UI fix that changed files, the functional revalidation follows the same project-commands, write-reconciliation, then fresh-verifier order. The final `done` or `failed` comes from the latest functional acceptance and task outcomes alone; fresh-verifier failure is part of functional acceptance, while UI residuals and `skipped` criteria never fail the run by themselves.

**7. Report and stop.** Fill `## Result`: each task's compact outcome, actual touched paths, and terminal output fingerprints; each acceptance command's exit result, compact output evidence, induced writes, and terminal fingerprints; reconciled commit-range receipts and attribution; the fresh verifier's conclusion; each acceptance criterion's `pass`, `fail`, or `skipped` status (with the reason when skipped); overlap-preservation evidence; ignored-path coverage; UI warnings if any; and whether functional acceptance ran. Include scope drift with how it was resolved, blocked dependents, prior-run carryover, and separately authorized actions when present. Record the acceptance fingerprint as a workspace fingerprint anchored to the immutable original base commit and final reconciled `HEAD`, plus complete ignored-path coverage and the exact UTF-8-byte-sorted union of every path whose index or worktree state differs from the original base and every expected, tolerated, committed, or actual touched path, including ignored output, empty directories, untracked, deleted, mode-changed, and type-changed paths, with each path's full `xsk-execute-plan-path-state-v1` fingerprint. Exclude Git metadata and run artifacts only after the protected anchor matches, but include `.xsk/.gitignore` when changed. A later comparison must match the anchor, original base, final reconciled `HEAD`, exact path set, and every entry; an added or missing path is a mismatch. Reuse later requires this fingerprint and the input identity to match. Produce an acceptance fingerprint only when ignored-path coverage is footprint or repository-wide, the latest functional acceptance passed, all other scope-verification evidence is conclusive, every task is terminal, the evidence anchor matches, and the final status is `done`. Incomplete ignored-path coverage always writes `Acceptance fingerprint: not produced`. Any other unmet condition does the same; set `status: failed` for an actual functional, scope-verification, or evidence-integrity failure. Incomplete coverage alone may leave otherwise successful tasks and observable checks at `status: done`, but the report must label the result unverified and non-reusable rather than treating missing evidence as a failure or a pass. Anchored terminal task checkpoints are still required. Do not commit, push, or publish unless the user asks for it. Stop.

## Output

A per-task list of compact results, actual touched paths, and terminal output fingerprints; each verification command's exit result and the writes it induced; any reconciled commit-range receipts and their attribution; the fresh verifier's conclusion; the acceptance report with each criterion's `pass`, `fail`, or `skipped` status (including a reason for `skipped`), overlap-preservation evidence, ignored-path coverage with its scope bound stated, scope drift, prior-run carryover and UI warnings if any, and whether functional acceptance ran; and the ledger path `.xsk/runs/<slug>.md` with its final `status` (`done` or `failed`), its evidence-anchor state, and either its acceptance fingerprint or `Acceptance fingerprint: not produced`.
